newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistan government under fire over Kansi snatch.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan government under fire over Kansi snatch.

text.p: The Pakistani government came under fire on Friday for apparently letting the United States spirit out of the country the man alleged to have carried out a deadly shooting outside CIA headquarters over four years ago.
Mystery shrounds this week's capture of Mir Aimal Kansi, accused of killing two Central Intelligence Agency employees and wounding three outside the CIA's home in Langley, Virginia.

Some politicians and newspapers have accused Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif's government of compromising national sovereignty by handing over a Pakistani citizen to a foreign government without fulfilling legal extradition procedures.

"Such behaviour from Pakistani authorities sends wrong signals not only to Washington but also to the rest of the world -- signals which may suggest that Pakistan can be taken for granted," The Nation newspaper said on Friday.
The Lahore-based daily, normally sympathetic to Sharif, a native of Lahore, said such behaviour was "quite alarming for a country which prides itself for its sovereignty".

The Pakistani Foreign Ministry cancelled its weekly news briefing on Thursday without explanation. Foreign Ministry, Interior Ministry and other government officials have refused to comment on the Kansi affair, as have U.S. diplomats based here.

The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI), announcing Kansi's capture, said on Tuesday that Kansi, who hails from Pakistan's southwestern province of Balochistan, had been delivered abroad by unidentified Afghan individuals to the custody of U.S. authorities and brought back to face trial.
FBI officials gave no details about Kansi's seizure and would not say if any of those involved would collect a reward of up to $2 million that had been offered for the wanted man.

"The names of those Afghans who, in collaboration with Pakistan's secret agencies, handed over Aimal Kansi to the FBI will be written in black words in the history of the independent world," Aurangzeb Kansi, leader of the Awami National Party (ANP) in Balochistan, said in a statement published on Friday.
The ANP is a junior partner in Sharif's ruling coalition.
Aurangzeb Kansi, a member of the famous Pashtun Kansi tribe like his detained namesake, said Islamabad's silence on the affair proved that the government had failed protect a citizen.

"There is now increasing evidence that Pakistan handed over Mir Aimal Kansi to a specially flown team of FBI and CIA agents by bypassing or underplaying the accused's legal and constitutuional rights," The Nation said on Friday.
Several newspapers argued that Pakistan's Extradition Act had been violated by not allowing Kansi the mandatory 15 days from his arrest to defend himself in a Pakistani court.
It is not clear whether Kansi was tracked down and seized inside Pakistan or in neighbouring Afghanistan.
A senior official of the purist Islamic Taleban militia, which controls more than two-thirds of Afghanistan, including areas bordering Balochistan, said he knew nothing of Kansi.
"We are interested in Afghan affairs and Kansi is not an Afghan issue," the official, Wakil Ahmad, told the Pakistan-based Afghan Islamic Press news service on Thursday.

The Karachi-based Dawn newspaper reported on Friday that military commandos accompanied by an unidentified foreigner had whisked a bearded young man from the Shalimar hotel in the remote Punjab provincial town of Dera Ghazi Khan early on Sunday morning.
But it said it could not confirm that Kansi was the man.
